title: Beige Book — September 2, 2026
html:
Official report: Summary · Full PDF Local PDF: 2026-09-02 Beige Book.pdf

Overall economic activity

Activity rose modestly since early July. "Ten of the twelve Federal Reserve Districts reported growth" in the slight to moderate range, and two reported no change. Manufacturing picked up, led by defense and data center orders. Residential construction fell, while nonresidential construction rose, largely on data center projects. Agriculture improved slightly but remains strained, with livestock stronger than crops. Outlooks were positive overall but mixed by sector, with concern about energy prices, policy, and international conflict. The report was prepared at the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis.

Consumer spending

Consumer spending edged up: price-sensitive shoppers were offset by solid high-end purchases. Auto sales were weak.

Labor markets

Employment rose very slightly. Hiring was strongest in manufacturing, construction, and some services, while demand for retail and hospitality workers fell. Skilled trades and technical workers were hard to find. Districts reported both positive and negative effects from artificial intelligence on labor demand. Wage growth was modest to moderate, with the largest increases in construction and manufacturing.

Prices

Prices rose moderately in most Districts. Input costs for energy, transportation, metals, and petrochemicals climbed sharply in manufacturing and construction. Tariffs continued to affect retail and manufacturing, and health care and insurance costs were a broad pressure. Some consumer-facing firms could not fully pass on higher costs because customers were price-sensitive.

Notable themes

  • Data centers and defense: leading manufacturing and nonresidential construction.
  • Energy costs: sharp input cost increases and a top outlook concern.
  • Tariffs: still affecting retail and manufacturing.
  • AI: mixed effects on labor demand.
  • Housing: residential construction fell.
  • Drought: a concern for agriculture in some Districts.

District highlights

  • Boston: Slight growth; strong consumer spending in some areas, weaker elsewhere.
  • New York: Modest growth led by manufacturing; input prices rose strongly.
  • Philadelphia: Modest growth and hiring; wage and price increases eased slightly.
  • Cleveland: Modest growth driven by manufacturing; consumer spending declined for a fourth period.
  • Richmond: Moderate expansion led by consumer travel and experiential spending; other sectors flat to slightly down.
  • Atlanta: Modest growth; lending up modestly.
  • Chicago: Slight growth; manufacturing up modestly; financial conditions tightened slightly.
  • St. Louis: Modest growth; prices rose robustly; outlook slightly improved.
  • Minneapolis: Slight growth and hiring; consumer spending fell; drought worried farmers.
  • Kansas City: Little change; softening conditions and inventory drawdowns; labor the top growth constraint.
  • Dallas: Moderate expansion; manufacturing, banking, and energy grew; drought hurt agriculture.
  • San Francisco: Little changed; staffing steady; residential real estate declined somewhat.

Read-through for SPY

  • Growth remains positive but uneven, with AI/data center and defense capex doing the heavy lifting.
  • Sharp energy and materials input costs plus limited pricing power for consumer firms keep margin risk in focus.
  • Weak autos, falling residential construction, and softer retail/hospitality hiring are pockets of weakness to watch.
